8e37ec89a058e3a46c1b9d2a72834771630f2827.summary: F-Secure announced in July 2013 a Mac OS X trojan, Janicab, disguised as a PDF. It uses a right-to-left override character so the name hides a .app extension, and it is code-signed, so Mac OS X runs it after one approval. It installs components in a hidden folder in the home directory, creates a cron job, contacts a command server, and takes screenshots and records audio. Most antivirus software did not detect it at the time. A later update says the developer certificate was revoked. The post gives removal steps and warns users to back up first.

8e3cb1df4bfe919159e8adeff374e65f8a3d913c.summary: Malware family entry for HyperBro, a remote access trojan (RAT) that the entry says has been observed to target primarily gambling industries, though it has been seen elsewhere too. It typically has 3 or more components, including a genuine loader and an encrypted, compressed payload with C2 information hardcoded. The entry lists vendor and agency report titles from 2018 to 2023 that tie HyperBro to APT27, Iron Tiger, LuckyMouse, UNC215, BRONZE UNION and Emissary Panda, alongside PlugX, Cobalt Strike and MimiKatz.

8ea37950ea1dfb7a966d0e8a5abaa4dc8d13d970.summary: Malwarebytes Threat Intelligence describes a March 2022 spear phishing campaign against Russian citizens and government entities. Lures impersonated Russian ministries and warned of banned services. Attached RTF files used a CVE-2021-40444 exploit to deliver Cobalt Strike. A separate actor, possibly linked to Carbon Spider, deployed a PowerShell-based RAT. Mustang Panda, UNC1151 and SCARAB are named as APT actors using war-related lures around Ukraine. Attribution is hedged throughout.
